title: Bo: this month is yours (Exodus 12:1–2)
hook: the first command to the whole people is to mark time by the new moon

segments.voice: Yesterday, the darkness you could feel, and homes that still had light. Your line was see your brother. Did you check on someone? Today, still in Bo, the moon. Day three hundred thirty-five.

Look at a work schedule someone else wrote for you. Shifts, breaks, the hour you may leave. Now imagine that for your whole life, and your parents' lives, every hour belonged to someone else. That's slavery's calendar: the master owns the clock. The plagues are almost over. One more, the worst, is coming. And right here, before anyone has left Egypt, God gives Moses and Aaron the first command meant for the whole people. You might expect something about freedom, or worship, or the law. It's about the moon.
screen: `A SCHEDULE SOMEONE ELSE WROTE.` → `THE MASTER OWNS THE CLOCK.` → `THE FIRST COMMAND: THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year to you." The Hebrew word for month is chodesh, and Jewish tradition hears in it chadash, new. A month is a new moon, a renewal. Tradition draws the Jewish calendar from that verse: months by the moon, kept in step with the sun so the spring festival stays in spring. In ancient times the new month was declared by a court in Jerusalem, after witnesses came to say they had seen the thin new crescent. Tradition says the calendar was later fixed by calculation, which is how it runs today. And the first day of each month, Rosh Chodesh, is still marked with extra prayers. Rashi, the medieval commentator, opens his whole commentary on the Torah with a question about this verse. Why, he asks, didn't the Torah simply begin here, with this month, the first command given to Israel? He has his own answer, about the land. But his question tells you how weighty this verse was to him. Sforno, a later Italian commentator, noticed the small word unto you. Until now, he says, their days belonged to others. From here on, the months are theirs. Before a free people can do anything else, it has to own its time.
screen: `THIS MONTH SHALL BE UNTO YOU.` · `CHODESH: MONTH, FROM NEW.` · `WITNESSES, THEN A FIXED CALENDAR.` · `SFORNO: THE MONTHS ARE YOURS.` · then, large: `OWN YOUR TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: claim today. Settle, and breathe. Say today's date to yourself, the day of the week, the month, the year. Not as a deadline. As a fact you're choosing to notice. Then ask: which hours today are mine to shape? Maybe not many. Maybe ten minutes on a bus. Pick one stretch and decide, now, what it's for. If you know the Hebrew date, say that too. If you pray, you can offer that stretch of time. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Our portion still. Today, its first command to a people not yet free: count your months by the new moon. Time becomes theirs.
Your line: own your time. Today, mark the date on purpose: write it at the top of a page, or look up at the moon tonight and see where it is. Day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Jews mark Rosh Chodesh, the new month, with added prayers including Hallel, and in synagogue the coming new month is announced on the Shabbat before. Some people also say a blessing over the waxing moon each month, Kiddush Levanah.

notes: Exodus 12:2 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (KJV is identical in wording); verify punctuation.
Sforno on 12:2: paraphrased as 'until now their days belonged to others; from here on the months are theirs.' Confirm this is a fair summary.
Rashi's answer (the land: 'the power of His works He declared to His people', Psalm 111:6) is mentioned only as 'about the land'.
Calendar history: witnesses before the Sanhedrin (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2); fixed calculated calendar traditionally attributed to Hillel II, 4th century. The script does not give a date.
Rosh Chodesh prayers: Hallel (partial) and Musaf; Kiddush Levanah in howItsDone. Check phrasing.
Editor review: the chodesh/chadash link and the later fixed calendar now framed as tradition; cut 'the great' for Rashi and the sixteenth-century date for Sforno.
